papers.title_in_file: Leveraging Analog Quantum Computing with Neutral Atoms for Solvent Configuration Prediction in Drug Discovery
papers.version_note: arXiv 2309.12129v2 (22 Sep 2023). The PDF holds the main text (pages 1 to 19, with the figures on pages 11 to 19) and a Supplementary Information (pages 20 to 28, with its own page numbers 1/9 to 9/9). The main text cites the SI sections as 'Section ??' (unresolved cross references).

figures.shows: Layout of optical traps of the neutral atom QPU: open circles on a triangular-type lattice; x axis QPU coordinate x in um (about -20 to about 20), y axis QPU coordinate y in um (about -17 to about 17); about 7 rows of traps, no data series.
figures.confirmed_by: The machine employs arrays of Rubidium atoms arranged in arbitrary 2D configurations defined by a layout of optical traps of the type shown in Fig. 1.

figures.shows: Schematic adiabatic path against normalized time s (0 to 1). Top: Rabi frequency (arbitrary units) rises linearly from 0 to its maximum at s about 0.25, stays flat until s about 0.75, then falls linearly to 0 at s = 1. Bottom: three detunings (arbitrary units) start at the same negative value, stay flat until s about 0.25, ramp up to three different final values (labelled Delta final) at s about 0.75 and stay flat; two end above zero and one below zero.
figures.confirmed_by: A schematic example of Ωi(s) and ∆i(s) is shown in Fig. 2.

figures.shows: Pipeline picture: (a) a 3D-RISM density as a closed isosurface; (b) a stack of six 2D density slices through the cross-section of the density; (c) three panels for one slice: the density map, a regular mesh of traps laid over it, and the few trap sites kept as qubits where the density is high.
figures.confirmed_by: The process is depicted schematically in Fig. 3.

figures.shows: Six 2D density slices (Register 0 to Register 5) with colour bars (density values about 0 to about 0.016 for Register 0, to about 0.040 for Registers 1 and 2, about 0.035 for Register 3, about 0.028 for Register 4, about 0.025 for Register 5) and red dots marking the chosen qubits; axes in 3D-RISM grid units (0 to about 90). Registers have 4 to 14 qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: The density slices with associated qubit registers are shown in Fig. 4.

figures.shows: Six panels of the trap layout of Figure 1 (open circles) with the qubits of each register of Figure 4 filled blue, refitted on the QPU layout; axes QPU coordinate x and y in um (about -20 to about 20).
figures.confirmed_by: In order to mimic a physical implementation, we fit the registers in the same trap layout of Fig. 1, as shown in Fig. 5.

figures.shows: Six histograms (Register 0 to 5) of sample count (y) against sampled bitstring (x) for 1000 samples of the adiabatic local algorithm; the orange bar is the minimal-cost bitstring. Register 0: orange bar about 810 counts and is the tallest. Register 1: tallest bar about 800 counts, orange bar small (about 30). Registers 2 and 3: orange bar is not the tallest (tallest about 285 and about 265, orange about 245 and about 85). Register 4: tallest about 480, orange bar very small (about 10). Register 5: tallest about 770, orange about 165 and second tallest.
figures.confirmed_by: The fact the bitstring with the lowest cost is not always the most sampled one is a consequence of the differences between the low energy spectrum of problem and Rydberg Hamiltonians.

figures.shows: For registers 0, 2, 3 and 5: left, experimental projector expectation value; right, noisy simulation with epsilon = 2.0% and epsilon' = 15.0%; x axis time (ns) about 500 to 1100, y axis detuning (rad/us) about -4 to -11. Colour scale maxima: register 0 about 0.25, register 2 about 0.05, register 3 about 0.04, register 5 about 0.12. Experiment and simulation show similar coarse structure.
figures.confirmed_by: The experimental measurements of the projector for all four registers are shown in Fig. 7, together with theoretical expectations given a reasonable estimate for false positive and false negative error rates on the machine.

figures.shows: (a) Sketch of the 4-atom register (q0 to q3, nearest-neighbour distance 5 um) with the two-level scheme and the r to the minus six interaction. (b) Four stacked panels, one per qubit, of the occupation expectation value against time (0 to about 1.1 us) at fixed detuning Delta/2pi = -0.87 MHz: noiseless simulation (dashed), noisy simulation (line) and experimental points with error bars; occupation oscillates with a first peak near 0.25 us at about 0.25 and a second smaller peak near 0.7 us; noisy simulation lies below the noiseless one and the experimental points follow the noisy line.
figures.confirmed_by: An example of fitting curves at a given detuning ∆ for the first register is shown in Fig. 8.

figures.shows: (a) MUP-I pocket with ligand and 3D-RISM isodensity wireframe; (b) zoom on the two crystal waters with two isosurfaces; (c) smoothed density slice with 6 qubits (colour bar about 0 to about 0.0023); (d) bar chart of counts against bitstring for the VQA emulation: tallest bar (101001) about 40, second (010100) about 28, then about 20, 19, 17, 12, 11 and 10.
figures.confirmed_by: In Fig. 10 we report the best water molecules configuration found by the algorithm (cyan atoms), corresponding to the best bitstring |101001⟩ found in the optimization.

figures.shows: Molecular rendering of the MUP-I binding pocket: red crystal-water oxygens, three cyan water molecules placed by the algorithm lying close to the red ones, and the 3D-RISM isosurface in wireframe.
figures.confirmed_by: In Fig. 10 we report the best water molecules configuration found by the algorithm (cyan atoms), corresponding to the best bitstring |101001⟩ found in the optimization.

figures.shows: (a) 16 numbered qubit positions on a grid, x and y in um (about -11 to about 11 and about -8 to about 8). (b) 2D synthetic density (colour bar about 0.001 to about 0.007) with three red gaussian centres and blue dots for the retained qubits.

figures.shows: (a), (b) two 2D synthetic densities with blue qubits and red gaussian centres; (c), (d) bar charts of sampled bitstring counts. In both, the red bar (the right placement) is the third tallest; the two tallest bars (green) are about 3.7 and about 3.5 thousand counts in (c) and about 3.8 and about 2.6 thousand in (d), the red bar about 1.5 thousand in (c) and about 0.7 thousand in (d).
figures.confirmed_by: The corresponding states obtained for the two test systems are reported in 2 c and d.

figures.shows: Percent of the best qubit-string (BS) in the optimized wave function (y) for four optimizers (Dummy, Forest, GBRT, GP) and two values of m. (a) m = 3 and 5: Dummy about 86 and about 79; Forest about 98 and about 94; GBRT about 98 and about 88 (large error bar); GP about 99 and about 99. (b) all optimizers about 54 to about 63. (c) m = 8 and 5: about 8 to about 21. (d) m = 25 and 15: about 14 to about 24. Error bars shown.

papers.what_it_is: A Pasqal and Qubit Pharmaceuticals paper that casts water placement in protein cavities (from 3D-RISM densities) as an Ising problem and tests a local adiabatic algorithm (emulated, with a simplified run on a Pasqal neutral atom QPU) and a global-laser variational algorithm (emulated).

existing.note: Text is on p.7 (the section heading starts on p.6). The paper also says on p.5 that the local algorithm cannot run on the current QPU because of the lack of local addressing.
quotes: technical limitations of the present hardware prevent us from using a local Hamiltonian as in equation (13)
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit in the section Beyond a Local Algorithm (p.7) and on p.5.

existing.note: The claim is stated as written. The paper gives its mechanism (the r to the minus six part of the Rydberg interaction, p.4) but runs no test that checks the guarantee. The claim also rests on a Rydberg blockade that holds for the chosen laser parameters.
quotes: thanks to the quantum nature of the algorithm, two water molecules are guaranteed to never be placed too close to each other
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the paper has no experiment that tests it.

existing.note: The QPU run was a simplified setting: a constant global pulse on the registers, checked against the emulated solution (p.6), not the full local algorithm. The text says the experiment is only 'compatible' with emulation on a qualitative level.
existing.value: The authors state that, as a proof of concept, both algorithms were shown to locate density maxima in non-trivial densities, and that a more simplified version was implemented on a real neutral atom QPU, where the experiments are, on a qualitative level, compatible with the theoretical predictions obtained from emulation.
existing.anchor: Conclusion and perspectives, p.8; Experimental measurement on QPU, p.6
quotes: As a proof of concept, both algorithms have been shown to successfully be able to locate density maxima in non-trivial densities.
A more simplified version was implemented on a real neutral atom QPU
On a qualitative level, the experiments can be seen to be compatible with theoretical predictions obtained from emulation.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

existing.note: The paper gives three reasons for the limit of 14: the machine layout, the state vector emulation limit and the need to couple Pulser with the QPU.
quotes: Presently, we limited ourselves to a qubit count of 14.
roughly 16 qubits can be emulated easily with Pulser
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit in Conclusion and perspectives (p.8).

assertions.value: The authors assume that each water molecule randomly oscillates around a definite stable position in the protein cavity, so that the three-dimensional RISM density is read as a sum of Gaussians and the placement problem becomes the search for the best Gaussian mixture.
assertions.anchor: A quantum Ising model formulation, p.2
quotes: In order to do so, we assume that each water molecule randomly oscillates around a definite stable position in the protein cavity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as the ansatz of its formulation (p.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that the L2 norm between the three-dimensional RISM density and the sum of placed Gaussians expands to the energy of a classical Ising model with exponentially decaying interactions.
assertions.anchor: A quantum Ising model formulation, p.3
quotes: Expanding the square, one sees that I2 defines the energy of an Ising model
Equation (3) is therefore a classical Ising model with exponentially decaying interactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper derives the form in equations (1) to (7), Section 2, p.3; the quoted lines state it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the water placement problem requires two water molecules to be placed at a minimal physical distance from each other, an extra constraint on the Ising model.
assertions.anchor: A quantum Ising model formulation, p.3
quotes: In addition, the water placement problem requires two water molecules to be placed at a minimal physical distance from each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as part of its problem definition (p.3).

assertions.value: The authors state that, when each atom is a graph vertex and vertices closer than a threshold are joined by an edge, the ground state of the Rydberg Hamiltonian at zero Rabi frequency and positive detuning is a solution to the Maximum Independent Set problem.
assertions.anchor: Analog quantum computing with neutral atoms, p.2
quotes: the ground state is a solution to the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem20, i.e. the problem of selecting the largest number of vertices in a graph that are not connected to each other directly by an edge.
assertions.certainty_reason: A relation the paper states with a citation, not proved in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Rydberg interaction decays as a power law while the problem Hamiltonian interaction decays exponentially, and that the proximity constraint between neighbouring excitations is taken care of by the r to the minus six part of the Rydberg Hamiltonian.
assertions.anchor: Solving the quantum Ising problem with a local Rydberg Hamiltonian, p.4
quotes: in the Rydberg Hamiltonian Uij decays as a power-law, while in the problem Hamiltonian Vij decays exponentially.
(10) does not directly encode the proximity constraint between neighbouring excitations, which is taken care of precisely by the r−6 part of the Rydberg Hamiltonian.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of the authors, not tested against a measurement in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The two interaction forms differ, so the Rydberg system only approximates the problem Hamiltonian.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum adiabatic evolution algorithm cannot be implemented on the current generation of neutral atom QPUs because of the lack of local addressing, and can only be tested with the Pulser classical emulator.
quotes: QAE, however, cannot be implemented on the current generation of neutral atom QPUs because of the lack of local addressing.
Nevertheless, the QAE algorithm, described in Algorithm 1, can be still tested using the Pulser classical emulator 24.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit on p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the local algorithm was emulated on six two-dimensional slices of the three-dimensional RISM density of the major urinary protein pocket, separated by a spacing of 0.5 Å, using 4 to 14 qubits.
assertions.anchor: Local algorithm emulation using 3D-RISM densities, p.5
quotes: separated by a spacing of 0.5 Å, for a total of 6 different slices
Overall, this test implementation requires 4 to 14 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own test setup on p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that current neutral atom quantum computers can only operate on two-dimensional qubit registers, so the three-dimensional three-dimensional RISM density is cut into two-dimensional slices and the algorithm is applied to each slice separately.
assertions.anchor: Local algorithm emulation using 3D-RISM densities, p.5
quotes: current generation neutral atom quantum computers can only operate on two-dimensional qubit registers
we apply the algorithm separately to each slice
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit and its workaround on p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the detunings are computed from the one-body coefficients by a heuristic mapping: each coefficient is shifted to be centred around the mean of its neighbours within the blockade distance, then rescaled so that the maximum corresponds to a fixed value.
quotes: by using the following heuristic mapping:
First, each Γi is shifted so that it is centered around the mean value of neighbouring nodes, obtaining the intermediate detunings ∆˜ i.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the mapping in equation (15) and the text after it (p.5-6).

assertions.value: The authors report that, for each register, the adiabatic dynamics were simulated with Pulser, the final state was sampled 1000 times, the minimal-cost sampled bitstring was selected as the solution, and the lowest-cost bitstring is not always the most sampled one.
assertions.anchor: Local algorithm emulation using 3D-RISM densities, p.6
quotes: We simulate the resulting adiabatic dynamics with Pulser, and sample the final state 1000 times.
The fact the bitstring with the lowest cost is not always the most sampled one is a consequence of the differences between the low energy spectrum of problem and Rydberg Hamiltonians.
assertions.certainty_reason: An emulation result from one study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 6: for the first register the minimal-cost bitstring (orange) is the most sampled, with about 810 of the 1000 samples; for the third, fourth and fifth registers it is not, and in the fifth register it is among the least sampled, with about 10 counts against about 480 for the most sampled.
assertions.anchor: Figure 6, p.15; Local algorithm emulation, p.6
quotes: Histogram of 1000 samples of the quantum state obtained with the local algorithm based on adiabatic evolution.
The fact the bitstring with the lowest cost is not always the most sampled one is a consequence of the differences between the low energy spectrum of problem and Rydberg Hamiltonians.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from a figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the QPU experiment each register was reproduced on the QPU and measured after a constant global laser pulse, and that the expectation value of the projector on the emulated solution was evaluated in a plane of detuning and pulse duration, with each point averaged over roughly 500 measurements.
quotes: The qubit register is then reproduced in the QPU, and its quantum state is measured after evolving under a constant global laser pulse.
Each point in the 2D plane is calculated as an average over roughly 500 measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental protocol on p.6.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on a qualitative level, the experiments are compatible with theoretical predictions obtained from emulation, and that this indicates meaningful solutions to the water placement problem belong to the space of physically allowed configurations of the QPU.
quotes: On a qualitative level, the experiments can be seen to be compatible with theoretical predictions obtained from emulation.
These results indicate that meaningful solutions to the water placement problem belong to the space of physically allowed configurations of the QPU.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, judged qualitatively.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantitative agreement measure (a distance or a fit statistic) is reported for the comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiment shows probability landscapes in this simplified setting can be accurately resolved by the machine, even without error correction or error mitigation, and that the probabilities involved are capped at only a few percent in certain systems.
quotes: the experiment shows that probability landscapes in this simplified setting can be accurately resolved by the machine, even in the absence of error correction or error mitigation techniques.
the small magnitude of the involved probabilities that are capped at only a few percent in certain systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; no accuracy measure is given.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 7: the experimental projector expectation values on the four registers shown have colour scale maxima of about 0.25, about 0.05, about 0.04 and about 0.12 in the order shown, over pulse durations of about 500 ns to about 1100 ns and detunings of about -4 rad/us to about -11 rad/us, with the noisy simulation showing a similar coarse pattern.
assertions.anchor: Figure 7, p.16; Experimental measurement on QPU, p.6
quotes: The experimental measurements of the projector for all four registers are shown in Fig. 7, together with theoretical expectations given a reasonable estimate for false positive and false negative error rates on the machine.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure labels the registers 0, 2, 3 and 5 while its caption numbers the solutions 1 to 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that calibration of the control devices gives static uncertainties of about 1% in the global spacing of the atomic array and about 4% in the spatial homogeneity of the Rabi frequency, and that laser intensity fluctuations cause a shot-to-shot variation of the Rabi frequency of about 5%.
quotes: static uncertainties in global spacing of the atomic array (≈ 1%) or in the spatial homogeneity of Ω on this array (≈ 4%)
fluctuations of laser intensity induces a shot-to-shot variation of Ω (≈ 5%)
assertions.certainty_reason: Device parameters reported by the vendor's own team for its own machine.

assertions.value: The authors report that the effective noise parameters found by fitting are an effective decay rate over 2 pi of 0.05 MHz, a false positive detection error of 2% and a false negative detection error of 18%.
quotes: the remaining effective noise parameter are found to be Γeff /2π = 0.05 MHz, ε = 2% and ε′ = 18%.
assertions.certainty_reason: A fitted result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The Figure 7 caption and plot titles use a false negative error of 15% (0.15), not the 18% the text reports; the paper does not say why.

assertions.value: The authors state in the caption of the experiment-versus-simulation figure that the classical simulation of the Rydberg Hamiltonian uses measurement errors of 0.02 and 0.15 for the probabilities of false positive and false negative detection.
quotes: measurement errors ϵ = 0.02 and ϵ′ = 0.15 related to the probability of false positive and false negative detect
assertions.certainty_reason: A setup value for one simulation that differs from the text on p.6.
assertions.reader_inference: This value differs from the 18% in the main text on p.6.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 8: for a fixed detuning over 2 pi of -0.87 MHz on the first four-qubit register, the site occupations oscillate with time up to about 0.25, the noisy simulation lies below the noiseless one, and the experimental points with error bars follow the noisy simulation.
assertions.anchor: Figure 8, p.17; Experimental measurement on QPU, p.6
quotes: For a fixed detuning ∆/2π = −0.87 MHz, the expectation value of the occupation of each qubit site, ⟨ni⟩, is plotted for noiseless simulation (dashed), noisy simulation (line) and experimental data (dot).
Overall, given the experimental errors sources that were discussed, the experimental data appear fully compatible with the emulated ones (see Fig. 7 and 8)
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from a figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given the experimental error sources discussed, the experimental data appear fully compatible with the emulated ones, confirming the viability of the proposed approach on an actual cold atom device.
quotes: the experimental data appear fully compatible with the emulated ones (see Fig. 7 and 8) confirming the viability of the proposed approach on an actual cold atom device.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim, with no quantitative test.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls the agreement qualitative on the same page, and 'fully compatible' is the stronger wording.

assertions.value: The authors state that in classical approaches such as Placevent and GAsol the minimal distance between water molecules is imposed by hand, with the risk of suboptimal local solutions or non-ergodicity.
quotes: a constraint that is imposed by hand in classical approaches such as Placevent26 or GAsol27 with the risk of incurring in suboptimal local solutions or non-ergodicity.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about other work, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the variational algorithm uses a global Rydberg Hamiltonian and minimizes the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian over the laser parameters, so that the algorithm belongs to the variational quantum algorithm family.
quotes: through emulation, we can still plan for an algorithm that will be able to run on more short-term devices using a global Rydberg Hamiltonian
This algorithm is therefore part of the Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) family
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the algorithm in equations (16) and (17) and Algorithm 2 (p.7).

assertions.value: The authors state that the variational algorithm, tested on simple synthetic densities, gives the correct positions of the Gaussian distribution centroids, and that tests on larger systems were not possible because of the high computational cost of emulating the time-dependent Schroedinger equation.
quotes: They show that the algorithm is able to give the correct positions of the Gaussian distributions centroids.
Due to the high computational cost involved in the emulation of a numerical solution of the time-dependent Shrödinger equation, we could not extend our tests towards larger systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An emulation result from one study, and the paper states the limit on test size.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on one six-qubit slice of the three-dimensional RISM density, 50 cycles of Bayesian optimization were run with 200 samples per wavefunction and a uniform variance of 5 (a.u.), and the best bitstring found was 101001.
quotes: We perform 50 cycles of Bayesian optimization, using 200 samples to represent each wavefunction produced by the corresponding set of laser parameters.
an uniform variance σ2 = 5 (a.u.)
corresponding to the best bitstring |101001⟩ found in the optimization
assertions.certainty_reason: An emulation result from one slice in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is for one slice of six, and the quality of the placement against the crystal waters is shown only in the Figure 10 picture.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 9 panel d: in the 6-qubit variational emulation without noise, the most sampled bitstring 101001 has about 40 counts and the second, 010100, about 28 counts, followed by six bitstrings with about 10 to about 20 counts each.
quotes: Histograms reporting the 6-qubit quantum state composition, in terms of basis stats, as obtained from the VQA emulated through Pulser on CPU, without noise
corresponding to basis states 101001 (first most sampled) and 010100 (second most sampled)
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The text on p.8 names the second state 010100 and a third state 010001, while the figure lists a different third bar; the counts total well below the 200 samples.

assertions.value: The authors state that the best configuration found by the variational algorithm places three water molecules, shown in the last main-text figure beside the crystal water molecules.
quotes: the cyan one are the three water molecules placed by the HQC algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: A result from one emulation in one study, shown as an image.
assertions.reader_inference: The pocket holds two crystal waters per p.5, and the algorithm places three; the paper gives no distance or accuracy measure against the crystal positions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the version implemented on a real neutral atom QPU represents, to the best of their knowledge, the first application of an analog quantum algorithm to the protein solvation problem.
quotes: which represents to the best of our knowledge the first application of an analog quantum algorithm to the protein solvation problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim by a team that includes the QPU vendor, not independently checked.

assertions.value: The authors state that the limit on the qubit count was constrained by the present machine layout, by the state vector emulation capabilities and by the need to couple Pulser and the actual QPU for the quantum adiabatic evolution model implementation.
quotes: This number was constrained by the present machine layout (see Fig. 1 and Fig. 5 ), by the state vector emulation capabilities
the need of coupling Pulser and the actual QPU for the quantum adiabatic evolution model implementation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the reasons in Conclusion and perspectives (p.8).

assertions.value: The authors state that future availability of time-dependent pulses and local addressing will remove the need of the Pulser emulation to prepare QPU data for the local algorithm, and that only time-dependent pulses are required for the variational version.
quotes: future availability of time-dependent pulses and local addressing will totally remove the need of the Pulser emulation to prepare QPU data.
only time-dependent pulses are required for the VQA version of Quantum-3D-RISM
assertions.certainty_reason: An author expectation about future hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that it will be interesting to compare the performances of the classical and quantum versions of 3D-RISM once the next QPU implementation allows tests at large scale, and that a careful study of the machine noise will be necessary.
quotes: it will be interesting to compare the performances of the classical and quantum versions of 3D-RISM
a careful study of the machine noise will be necessary
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as future work in Conclusion and perspectives (p.8); no comparison with classical 3D-RISM placement is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no benchmark of the quantum algorithms against a classical placement method.

assertions.value: The authors state that one key advantage of analog computing is relatively constant noise levels with increasing system size, which makes them optimistic about QPU simulations with a high number of qubits.
quotes: one key advantage of analog computing is to exhibit relatively constant noise levels with increasing system size making us optimistic about the prospect of QPU simulations encompassing a high number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own expectation, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that no widely accepted proof of exponential advantage for quantum computing calculations has yet been provided, and that a polynomial advantage could still give more accurate simulations on near-term devices.
quotes: no widely accepted proof of exponential advantage for quantum computing calculations has been yet provided
in practice, a polynomial advantage could still provide more accurate simulations at hand in near-term quantum devices
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to cited work, not tested in it.

assertions.value: The authors describe the Fresnel QPU as an industrial neutral atom QPU made of single 87Rb atoms trapped in arrays of optical tweezers, conceived and manufactured by Pasqal, with a two-photon excitation from 420-nm and 1013-nm laser beams through an intermediate state.
quotes: an industrial neutral atom QPU made of single 87Rb atoms trapped in arrays of optical tweezers, conceived and manufactured by PASQAL.
The first (respectively second) photon excitation is generated by a 420-nm (1013-nm) laser beam.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors report that for each of two synthetic densities 16 qubits were used, and that the quantum adiabatic evolution algorithm finds with a good probability the bitstring corresponding to the right placement of the Gaussian distributions in each mixture.
quotes: For each of case 16 qubits are used, placing them uniformely on the 2D densities.
the QAE algorithm is able to find, with a good probability, the bitstring corresponding to the right placement of the gaussian distributions in each mixture.
assertions.certainty_reason: An emulation result from one study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 2 of the Supplementary Information panels c and d: in both synthetic cases the bitstring that marks the right placement (red bar) is the third most sampled, behind two taller bars, with about 1.5 thousand counts against about 3.7 and about 3.5 thousand in panel c, and about 0.7 thousand against about 3.8 and about 2.6 thousand in panel d.
assertions.anchor: SI Figure 2, p.22; SI Section 1, p.21
quotes: The probability of those states best representing the gaussian component location is highlighted in red, in panel c and d.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from a figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls the probability 'good' while the right placement is not the most sampled bitstring in either panel.

assertions.value: The authors state that four Bayesian minimizers (Dummy, Forest, GBRT and GP) were tested, with m values between 3 and 25 and 200 Bayesian optimization cycles per emulated system, each cycle ideally corresponding to 200 measures on the real QPU.
quotes: We test the four different minimizers1 namely: i) Dummy, ii) Forest, iii) GBRT and iv) GP minimizer.
We tested m values between m = 3 and m = 25.
For each emulated system, 200 bayesian optimization cycles are performed.

papers.title_in_file: Graph Algorithms with Neutral Atom Quantum Processors
papers.version_note: arXiv 2403.11931v1 (18 Mar 2024). A review paper by Pasqal authors. Pages 1 to 14 are the text, pages 14 to 23 the references (a reference to a Pasqal MILP paper is joined to a stray 'Focustolearnmore.' string on p.22).
sections_read: 2 Graph Hamiltonians with interacting neutral atoms in tweezer arrays
Box 1 | Dealing with unsought terms in UD Graph embeddings
3.1 Solving the maximum independent set problem on unit-disk graphs
Box 3 | Improving addressability in analog neutral atom QPUs
4.2 Limitations and prospects for quantum GML

figures.shows: (a) Ising case: a graph of four nodes where an atom excited to a Rydberg state (black) blocks neighbours within the blockade radius r_b, before and after evolution under H_Ising. (b) XY case: an excitation hops along edges within radius r_e under H_XY. (c) Pipeline from a graph G with about 25 nodes to an embedded atom layout r_G (green discs) to an interaction matrix U(r_G) shown as a heat map (colour bar 0 to 1) that closely matches the adjacency matrix A_G (yellow diagonal-band pattern on a dark background).
figures.confirmed_by: In Figure 1(c), we show that the associated Ising interaction matrix closely reproduces the adjacency matrix of G, a UD graph.

figures.shows: (a) A non-planar graph (complete bipartite, K3,3) on the left, and its 3D embedding with chains of ancillary atoms on the right. (b) A crossing-edge gadget in 2D with grey nodes at detuning 2 delta and white nodes at detuning delta. (c) Geometric programming pipeline: a polynomial f(z) in binary variables is split into gadget atom clusters, assembled into an atomic register with local detunings delta_i, whose Hamiltonian spectrum has a low-energy solution band H_sol of width below epsilon, gapped from excited states by Delta E greater than 0.
figures.confirmed_by: addressed the MIS problem for the complete bipartite graph K3,3 using a 3D arrangement of qubits shown in Fig. 2(a), in conjunction with local detunings.

figures.shows: (a) A parameterized unitary U applied to atomic registers shaped as two unit-disk graphs G1 and G2, a measurement of an observable, and two different histograms of the observable distribution P_O (bars up to about 0.6 and about 0.7 on a 0 to 1 scale). (b) A graph with nodes labelled A, B, C (red, green, blue) addressed by node-specific local drives Omega_i(t) and delta_i(t) over time in microseconds.
figures.confirmed_by: To address this need, nodes with distinct labels in a graph can be managed with specific local controls, as illustrated in Fig. 3(b).

figures.shows: A graph G enters light preprocessing, then a QPU, then light postprocessing, giving regression, an optimal solution or a classification. Light iterative processing with a classical optimizer (QAOA, VQE, VQAA) sits above the QPU. Heavy classical blocks sit below: heavy preprocessing (train surrogate models, problem reduction, warm start; QEL), heavy iterative processing (decompose problem, solve sub-problem or master problem; CG, BP, Benders) and heavy postprocessing (feed to a neural network; transformers).
figures.confirmed_by: These algorithms require heavy classical computation, either at preprocessing (left) as detailed in 4.3, in iterative processes (center) as detailed in 5.1 or at post-processing (right) as detailed in 5.2.

papers.what_it_is: A Pasqal review of quantum algorithms for graph problems (optimization, graph machine learning and hybrid schemes) on neutral atom QPUs, with boxes on hardware progress; it reports no new measurements.

existing.note: Box 4 is on p.11 (the stored anchor says p.9-10; Section 4.2 on p.10 also names the low repetition rate as a limit). The paper gives the cycle steps: loading about 100 ms, arranging about 100 ms and imaging about 50 ms per shot.
quotes: reduces the repetition rate of the useful computation to few Hz.
In addition, the effective repetition rate is even scaled down by the finite probability of assembling a defect-free quantum register at each cycle.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit in Box 4 (p.11) and Section 4.2 (p.10).

existing.note: The statement is the authors' (Pasqal) projection of what combined hardware techniques should achieve; no measured rate is reported. The techniques are named in Box 4 (p.11).
quotes: Overall, the combination of all those techniques should raise the effective repetition rate to the 100 Hz or kHz range.
existing.certainty_reason: A projection by a vendor about its own technology, not tested in the paper.

existing.note: The abstract says the paper also clarifies ongoing hardware advancements, with an emphasis on scalability, controllability and repetition rate. The paper is a review and reports no new measurement.
quotes: In this paper, we review the advancements in quantum algorithms for graph problems running on neutral atom Quantum Processing Units (QPUs), and discuss recently introduced embedding and problem-solving techniques.
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's scope (p.1).

existing.note: The speedup is a result of the authors of Ref. [36], an experiment with more than 280 atoms; the paper cites it and does not run it. The same paragraph adds that Ref. [37] reached a quadratic speed-up over effective classical techniques by adding a local Hamiltonian.
quotes: For long enough evolution times, the authors experimentally identified a quadratic quantum speedup with respect to classical simulated annealing on hard graphs.
Intriguingly, the locality of UD-MIS makes it relatively easy to approximate classically, and there even exists a so-called polynomial-time approximation scheme

assertions.value: The authors state that one unique advantage of neutral atom technology is the ability to reconfigure the geometry of the qubit register from shot to shot, which makes possible the native embedding of graph-structured problems at the hardware level.

assertions.value: The authors state that for atoms with a ground state and a highly excited Rydberg state, two atoms in the Rydberg state interact through a van der Waals interaction scaling as C6 over r to the sixth power, giving an Ising Hamiltonian with a Rabi frequency term, a detuning term and pairwise additive interactions.
quotes: two atoms prepared in the |1⟩-state interact through a van der Waals interaction scaling as C6/r6, where r corresponds to the interatomic distance and C6 is a constant that depends on the chosen Rydberg level.
For a system of N atoms the van der Waals interactions are pairwise additive and contribute to the Ising Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the Ising Hamiltonian in equation (1) in Section 2 (p.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that under a resonant drive with constant Rabi frequency, two atoms separated by less than the Rydberg blockade radius, defined as r_b = (C6 over h-bar times the Rabi frequency) to the power one sixth, cannot both be excited at the same time.
quotes: Under resonant (δ = 0) drive with constant Rabi frequency Ω, two atoms separated by a distance smaller than the Rydberg blockade radius rb, defined as rb = (C6/ℏΩ)1/6, cannot be both excited at the same time (Fig. 1a).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the blockade radius in Section 2 (p.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that with qubit states encoded in two dipole-coupled Rydberg states the interaction gives an XY Hamiltonian whose exchange term is proportional to the inverse cube of the distance between two qubits, with a threshold distance r_e = (C3 over h-bar times the Rabi frequency) to the power one third above which resonant driving dominates.
quotes: The exchange term is proportional to the inverse cube of the distance between two qubits with coupling strength C3 which can also feature an angular dependency.
one can define a threshold distance re = (C3/ℏΩ)1/3 above which resonant driving dominates over the effect of spin-exchange.

figures.shows: Representative references for the use of different basis functions (Gaussians, plane waves, Bloch/Wannier functions, grids, pseudo-spectral or discrete variable representations) in first- and second-quantized quantum algorithms for the electronic structure problem; one cell is marked not yet studied.
figures.confirmed_by: A variety of functional forms have been considered for the electron orbitals (see Table 3 for a list of orbitals commonly considered in quantum computing).

figures.shows: Logical resource estimates for QPE on molecular systems (FeMo-co with 2196 qubits and 3.2 times 10 to the 10 gates by THC qubitization, or about 193 qubits and about 3 times 10 to the 12 gates by randomized compilation; cytochrome P450 with 1434 qubits and 7.8 times 10 to the 9 gates; lithium-ion battery molecules, chromium dimer, ruthenium catalyst, ibrutinib, molybdenum catalysts, amyloid beta fragment, cyclic ozone), with the number of samples (7 in most rows, about 600 for the randomized FeMo-co row, 3 to 9 for molybdenum).
figures.confirmed_by: We list state-of-the-art resource estimates and refer to the references therein for prior estimates.

figures.shows: Logical resource estimates for QPE on material systems (electron gas, lithium-ion battery materials, nickel/palladium oxide catalysts, magnesium/niobium alloys, nitrogen vacancy center in diamond), with logical qubit ranges from 100 to 500,000 and T or Toffoli gate counts per sample from 10 to the 8 to 10 to the 19, 7 samples each.
figures.confirmed_by: We list state-of-the-art resource estimates and refer to the references therein for prior estimates.

figures.shows: Circuit identity: the block-encoding U_AB of a product AB acts on s qubits using a + b ancilla qubits and one call to each of U_A and U_B, drawn as U_B and U_A stacked on the system register.

figures.shows: Circuit identity for the product block-encoding when U_A and U_B act on the same a ancilla qubits, using a + 1 ancilla qubits: U_B and U_A on the register with an a-controlled generalized Toffoli gate on an extra qubit and an X gate.
figures.confirmed_by: In fact, we can assume without loss of generality that a = b (by taking the maximum of the two) and improve the construction using the circuit in Fig. 2

figures.shows: Circuit identity: the tensor product block-encoding U_(A tensor B) uses U_A and U_B in parallel on separate registers with a + b ancilla qubits and one call to each.
figures.confirmed_by: The operation UA⊗B := (UA ⊗ UB) is an (αβ, a + b, αϵb + βϵa)-blockencoding of the operator A ⊗ B, as depicted in Fig. 3.

figures.shows: Circuit identity: the linear-combination block-encoding U_LC equals PREPARE, then SELECT acting on the ancilla register and the system, then PREPARE-dagger, using ceil(log2 L) + m ancilla qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: that is, ULC := PREPARE† · SELECT · PREPARE is a (λ, ⌈log2(L)⌉, 0)-block-encoding of the LCU i ciUi

figures.shows: An example qubitization circuit for a Hermitian (1, 3, 0) block-encoding U_A: a three-qubit register acted on by U_A followed by a reflection (minus Z gate) controlled on the three ancilla qubits.

figures.shows: The QSVT circuit U_Phi: a Hadamard on an extra qubit, alternating U_A and U_A-dagger on the register with m-controlled phase rotations e^(i phi Z) on the ancilla, and a final Hadamard; it block-encodes f(A) for a definite-parity polynomial f of degree d.
figures.confirmed_by: one can implement a block-encoding of f (A) using d/2 calls to UA, d/2 calls to UA† , 2d m-controlled Toffoli gates, and d single-qubit Z rotations (as shown in Fig. 6).

figures.shows: High-level comparison of Hamiltonian simulation techniques with qubits, access model, scaling, pros and cons: product formula of order k (O(n) qubits, Pauli or sparse access), qDRIFT (O(n) qubits), Taylor and Dyson series (O(n + log L) qubits, block-encoding access, scaling ||H||_1 t n L log(1/epsilon)), and QSP/QSVT (O(n + log L) qubits, scaling n L (||H||_1 t + log(1/epsilon))).
figures.confirmed_by: Each algorithm has its own advantages and disadvantages, as described at a high level in Table 6.

figures.shows: Quantum circuit for the QFT on n qubits: Hadamard gates and controlled phase shift gates R_2 to R_n in a triangular pattern, followed by swap gates that reverse the order of the output qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: the quantum circuit is given in Fig. 7 (see also [1, Fig. 5.1]), where N = 2n.

figures.shows: Quantum circuit for QPE: P ancilla qubits in |0> each prepared by a Hadamard and controlling U to the 2^p on the input state, followed by an inverse QFT and measurements of the P ancilla qubits, which give a P-bit estimate of the phase correct up to error O(2^-P) with high probability.
figures.confirmed_by: The quantum circuit for the standard approach to QPE is shown in Fig. 8.

figures.shows: A simple circuit to prepare an arbitrary 3-qubit state with non-negative real amplitudes using controlled Y rotations R_y(theta_s,p), with 2^n minus 1 angles for s in {0, ..., n-1} and p in {0, ..., 2^s minus 1}; negative or complex amplitudes need 2^n extra controlled phase gates.
figures.confirmed_by: This approach requires O(N ) n-qubit gates applied sequentially, as depicted in Fig. 9.

figures.shows: Asymptotic resource cost of exact state preparation of arbitrary states with CNOT and arbitrary single-qubit gates: circuit size O(2^n) in all rows, depth O(2^n/n) with no ancilla, depth O(2^n/(m + n)) with m ancillas up to O(2^n/n), and depth O(n) with O(2^n) ancillas.
figures.confirmed_by: In Table 7, we collect several state preparation results in the model where any single-qubit gate can be performed exactly and the only multiqubit gates allowed are CNOTs.

figures.shows: Asymptotic resource cost of approximate state preparation in the Clifford plus T gate set: circuit size about O(2^n log(2^n/epsilon)) or O(2^n log(1/epsilon)) or O(2^n log(n/epsilon)), with depth and ancilla tradeoffs, the last row reaching depth O(n + log(1/epsilon)) with O(2^n) ancilla qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: Results in this model are collected in Table 8.

figures.shows: Explicit resource counts for block-encoding arbitrary matrices of classical data: optimized for minimum depth about 4 N squared qubits, T-depth about 10 log N + 24 log(1/epsilon) and T-count about 12 N squared log(1/epsilon); optimized for minimum count about N log(1/epsilon) qubits, T-depth about 8 N + 12 log N (log(1/epsilon)) squared and T-count about 16 N log(1/epsilon) + 12 log N (log(1/epsilon)) squared.
figures.confirmed_by: We reproduce their resource counts optimized for minimum T -depth and for T -count in Table 9.

figures.shows: (a) A quantum circuit C with state preparation, unitary gates (CX and T) and measurements MZ and MX; (b) its fault-tolerant realization F(C) with every qubit replaced by a logical qubit and QEC gadgets interspersed between gadgets for each basic component.
figures.confirmed_by: see Fig. 10.

assertions.value: The authors state that nuclear physics presents a classically challenging quantum many-body problem that appears well suited to quantum computers, that nuclear Hamiltonians are typically more complex than electronic ones, and that future work should determine end-to-end resources including state preparation and observable measurement.

future work should determine the resources required for end-to-end simulations, including state preparation and measurement of observables.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' own statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that typical combinatorial optimization problems have limited structure to exploit, so quantum computing most often provides only polynomial speedups, with up to quadratic speedups via Grover's search algorithm for a wide variety of such problems.
quotes: Typical combinatorial optimization problems have limited structure to exploit, and therefore quantum computing most often only provides polynomial speedups.
for a wide variety of such problems, quantum computers do offer up to quadratic speedups via Grover’s search algorithm [1].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not cover quantum approaches for approximate combinatorial optimization (variational quantum algorithms or quantum annealing), which are heuristic, and that there is a general scarcity of concrete evidence that they will deliver practical advantages.
quotes: We do not specifically cover the large body of work on quantum approaches for approximate combinatorial optimization (typically variational quantum algorithms or quantum annealing).
these quantum algorithms are heuristic and there is a general scarcity of concrete evidence that they will deliver practical advantages.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' own statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that if there are at least m marked elements among N, search succeeds with high probability using a number of Grover iterations scaling as the square root of N over m, and that for SAT with n variables and l literals the overall gate complexity grows as (l + n) times the square root of the number of truth assignments.
quotes: by using O( N/m) Grover iterations.
giving an overall complexity of O((
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in amplitude amplification, if measuring the prior state yields a marked element with probability at least p, then O(sqrt(1/p)) Grover iterations suffice, each requiring a reflection about the prior state and a check of whether an element is marked.
quotes: then O( 1/p) “Grover iterations” suffice to find
The algorithm requires preparing the initial state |ψ⟩, and then each iteration consists of a reflection 2|ψ⟩⟨ψ| − I around |ψ⟩ and checking whether an element is marked (in superposition).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that studies of Grover-type quadratic or smaller speedups revealed that they are unlikely to be useful for the foreseeable future unless the large overheads of current fault-tolerant quantum computing schemes can be greatly reduced.
quotes: Unfortunately, these recent studies revealed that quadratic or smaller speedups alone are unlikely to be useful for the foreseeable future, unless the large overheads of current fault-tolerant quantum computing schemes can be greatly reduced.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors quote a cited study that, for constraint satisfaction problems solvable within one day, found potentially large quantum speedups, but that the quantum advantage disappears if one includes the cost of the classical processing power required to decode the surface code using current techniques.
quotes: In particular, the quantum advantage disappears if one includes the cost of the classical processing power required to perform decoding of the surface code using current techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most recent cited reference estimates that achieving a quantum advantage via a quadratic speedup requires at least a month-long computation already if each iteration contains at least one floating-point operation, and that cubic and quartic speedups look more promising but need techniques beyond Grover search.
quotes: estimates that achieving a quantum advantage via a quadratic speedup requires at least a month-long computation already if each iteration contains at least one floating-point operation.
The situation looks more promising for cubic and quartic speedups, but unfortunately such improvements seem to require techniques beyond Grover search.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the circuit model Grover search strictly gives a slowdown for database search, since the circuit would have gate complexity O(N^(3/2)), worse than going through the data in linear time O(N), and that the quadratic speedup is recovered only with a QRAM of constant or logarithmic cost per query.
quotes: strictly speaking Grover search gives a slowdown for database search, as every Grover iteration needs to “touch” every element in the database.
In the database scenario, we can only recover the quadratic speedup if we assume that we can use a quantum random access memory (QRAM), with constant (or logarithmic) cost for each database query.
Grover’s search circuit, on the other hand, would have gate complexity O(N 3/2)
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that Grover's algorithm can give a quadratic speedup without extra hardware assumptions when the elements searched can be generated and checked on the fly, as for SAT, which is the defining feature of problems in NP.
quotes: Grover’s algorithm can provide a quadratic speedup without extra hardware assumptions when the elements of the list that we search over can be easily generated and checked “on the fly.”
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for unstructured search exhaustive search is essentially the best classical approach, and that under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis the best classical algorithm for SAT has running time 2^(n - o(n)).
quotes: For the unstructured search problem, exhaustive search is essentially the best that can be done, with a running time ∼ ℓ · 2n.
under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis [12, 13] the best classical algorithm for SAT has running time 2n−o(n).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quadratic speedup of Grover search is optimal in the black-box query model, and that they do not expect a bigger than quadratic speedup in gate complexity in the general non-black-box case.
quotes: It can be shown that this speedup is optimal in the black-box query model [14].
we do not expect that there would be a bigger than quadratic speedup in gate complexity [15] in the general (non-black-box) case.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that since the best known 3-SAT solvers have complexity O(1.308^n), only slightly better than Schoening's O(1.334^n), amplitude amplification on Schoening's algorithm implies a close-to-quadratic quantum speedup, though this concerns worst-case complexity and practical instances can scale much better.
quotes: Since the best known 3-SAT solvers [16, 17] have complexity O(1.308n)—only slightly better than Scho¨ning’s O(1.334n) complexity—this implies a close-to-quadratic quantum speedup.
this relates to worst-case complexity, and on practical instances, the scaling can be much better.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for graph problems such as single-source shortest paths the quantum query complexity is Theta of sqrt(|V||E|) against classical O(|E|) queries, and that for similar problems such as connectivity and minimum spanning tree the speedup is similarly (sub)quadratic.
quotes: whereas the quantum query complexity of this problem is Θ(
For all of these problems, there is a similar (sub)quadratic quantum speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the traveling salesperson problem the best provable quantum speedup is only subquadratic, with a time complexity O(1.728^n) over the O(2^n) classical dynamic programming algorithm assuming unit-cost QRAM calls, and that it is one of the least likely candidates for a practical quantum speedup when nodes have large degree.
quotes: However, for this problem, the best provable speedup is only subquadratic.
resulting in time complexity O(1.728n) assuming that QRAM calls have unit costs.
the traveling salesperson problem seems to be one of the least likely candidates to achieve a practical quantum speedup when the nodes have large degree.
The best classical algorithm uses dynamic programming and runs in time O(2n).

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum walk algorithms for backtracking and branch-and-bound achieve an essentially quadratic speedup over classical backtracking, for instance finding exact ground states for most instances of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model in time O(20.226n) with a flat-printed exponent, and apply to mixed-integer programs including some portfolio optimization formulations.
quotes: The quantum algorithm can achieve an essentially quadratic speedup compared to its classical backtracking variant.
it can find exact ground states for most instances of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model [28] in time O(20.226n) [26]
Branch-and-bound-based speedups can also be applied to solve mixed-integer programs, which include certain formulations of the portfolio optimization problem [27].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum walk algorithms for element distinctness reduce queries from N to N^(2/3), but the algorithm needs a QRAM of roughly N^(2/3) registers storing data in superposition, making such algorithms often impractical because of space and gate overheads.
quotes: The query reduction is moderate N → N 2/3 in the number of elements N , but the corresponding quantum algorithm [21] unfortunately uses a QRAM consisting of roughly N 2/3 registers; moreover, the QRAM must be able to store data in superposition.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that resource estimates indicate early and intermediate-term fault-tolerant devices will fail to deliver practical advantages when the available speedup is only quadratic, due to intrinsic overheads of quantum computation, so identifying beyond-quadratic speedups is of principal importance.
quotes: resource estimates indicate that early and intermediate-term fault-tolerant devices will fail to deliver practical advantages when the available speedup is only quadratic, due to intrinsic overheads of quantum computation compared to classical computation
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that many proposals that could deliver superquadratic speedups, including the quantum adiabatic algorithm and QAOA, lack rigorous theoretical performance guarantees, and that it remains an open question whether quantum algorithms can provide superquadratic speedups for useful problems in exact combinatorial optimization.
quotes: Unfortunately, many proposals that could conceivably deliver superquadratic speedups lack rigorous theoretical performance guarantees.
Overall, it remains an open question whether quantum algorithms can provide superquadratic speedups for useful problems in exact combinatorial optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states this open question in Section 4.2 (p.81).

assertions.value: The authors define binary optimization as finding the bit string z* in {1, -1}^n minimizing a cost function C given by a compact description, assuming for simplicity that the minimizer is unique and the optimal value E* is known, and note that QUBO is degree-2, MAX-CUT is the degree-2 case with coefficients of zero or one and MAX-3-SAT is a sum of degree-3 terms.
quotes: The input to the problem is a compact description of some cost function C : {1, −1}n → R, and the desired output is the string z∗ for which C is minimized.
if C is a degree-2 polynomial in z, this is a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey defines the problem in Section 4.2 (p.81-82).

assertions.value: The authors state that a vanilla application of Grover's algorithm to binary optimization achieves O*(20.5n) running time (exponent printed flat), and that the three approaches covered require polynomial (linear) space while their running times are expected to scale exponentially in n.
quotes: A vanilla application of Grover’s algorithm to binary optimization problems achieves O∗(20.5n) running time
all of these algorithms require polynomial (in fact, linear O(n)) space.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors describe the QAOA as fixing a depth p and variational parameters, starting from the equal superposition state and alternating rotations about the cost function C and the mixing operator, with the expected repetitions to obtain z* equal to the inverse of the probability, quadratically sped up by amplitude amplification.
quotes: The QAOA starts in the n-qubit equal superposition state |+⟩⊗n and implements alternating rounds of rotations about the diagonal cost function C
this running time can be quadratically sped up by performing amplitude amplification on top of the QAOA protocol
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey defines the QAOA in Section 4.2 (p.83).

assertions.value: The authors state that the repetitions for the QAOA can be reduced to O(1) at the expense of taking p at least exponentially large in n, in which case the QAOA can be viewed as a Trotterized simulation of the adiabatic algorithm.
quotes: one can reduce the number of repetitions needed to O(1) at the expense of taking p to be very large (at least exponentially large in n); indeed, for sufficiently large p, the QAOA can be viewed as a Trotterized simulation of the adiabatic algorithm [4].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that a cited analytic formula for QAOA on hard k-SAT instances with constant p suggested, numerically, an average success probability behaving as 2^(-0.33n) for p equal to 10 on 8-SAT, but that this does not analytically imply an average running time of O*(2^(0.33n/2)) since the average of the inverse probability can be much larger than the inverse of the average.
quotes: suggested, for example, that the average success probability behaves as 2−0.33n for p = 10 on 8-SAT.
such a conclusion is not analytically supported as the average of the inverse probability can be much larger than the inverse of the average probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that numerical work on QAOA for the low autocorrelation binary sequences problem up to n equal to 40 provided further evidence that QAOA may be effective as an exact algorithm, although compared with the best classical heuristic solver the advantage appeared to be subquadratic.
quotes: numerically assessed the performance of QAOA on instances of the low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) problem up to n = 40, although compared to the best classical heuristic solver, the advantage appeared to be subquadratic.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum adiabatic algorithm's gate complexity scales at least as the inverse of the minimum spectral gap, that the expectation is that the minimum gap will be exponentially small in n, and that it remains possible that it surpasses the running time of Grover's algorithm in some cases and could deliver a superquadratic speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the short-path algorithm performs a pair of discrete jumps using quantum phase estimation and amplitude amplification, aims at a rigorous guarantee of finding z* in time 2^((0.5 - c)n) for some c above zero, and was shown for MAX-Ek-LIN2 instances to run in O*(2^((0.5 - c)n)) under conditions on the spectral density, though it remained unclear when those conditions are met.
quotes: The goal of these algorithms was to be able to provide a rigorous guarantee that the algorithm can find z∗ in time 2(0.5−c)n for some value of c > 0.
However, it remained unclear when these conditions were met.

assertions.value: The authors state that a dual version of the short-path algorithm was unconditionally shown to solve k-SAT in time O*(2^((0.5 - c)n)) for an extremely small constant c above zero, and the same for typical instances of the SK and p-spin models, a polynomial speedup over Grover's algorithm and superquadratic advantage over classical exhaustive search.
quotes: O∗(2(0.5−c)n) for a (extremely small) constant c > 0, and that the same is true for typical instances of the SK model and its higher-body generalization (p-spin model), a polynomial speedup over Grover’s algorithm and superquadratic advantage over classical exhaustive search.

assertions.value: The authors report that a cited compilation estimated that for an n equal to 512 instance of the SK model, a single QAOA step would require 577 logical qubits and 5.0 times ten to the fifth Toffoli gates, and that a rough breakeven estimate in another reference found a quartic speedup could break even in seconds to hours with classical parallelism.

assertions.value: The authors state that for most of the algorithms there is no provable beyond-Grover advantage, that in the case with a proof the size of the advantage is minuscule, and that prospects rest on extrapolations from very small simulated instances and physical speculation.
quotes: The most salient one is that for most of the algorithms above, there is no provable beyond-Grover advantage. Meanwhile, in the case of [8], the size of the provable beyond-Grover advantage is miniscule.

assertions.value: The authors state that an assumed polylog(N) cost of the dense block-encoding is only defensible if the key metric is circuit depth and many ancilla qubits are available, that the total gate complexity must be at least Omega(N squared), and that the normalization constant can introduce poly(N) factors into an end-to-end analysis.

This is only defensible if the key metric is the circuit depth and if many ancilla qubits are available.

The complexity of QLSSs depends on the condition number κ(A) = A−1 · ∥A∥ of the matrix A
together with an (α, a, 0)-block-
