assertions.value: The authors state that the query complexity of QLSSs has a known lower bound of Omega(kappa(A)), that methods with linear dependence on kappa' are called optimal and those with kappa' times a polylogarithm near-optimal, where kappa' equals kappa times alpha, and that a complexity linear in kappa and logarithmic in the inverse error is claimed to be jointly optimal.
quotes: where a lower bound of Ω(κ(A)) is known; see [4, 5].
Methods achieving O(κ′(A)) dependence are termed “optimal” and methods achieving κ′(A) polylog(κ′(A)) are termed “near-optimal.”
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states the lower bound and the optimality terminology in Section 18 (p.288).

assertions.value: The authors state that the first optimal QLSS prepares an ansatz state with overlap squared at least 1/2 using at most O(kappa') queries by discrete adiabatic methods and then refines it by eigenstate filtering at additional cost O(kappa' log(1/epsilon)), succeeding with probability at least 1/2, with expected query count Q equal to kappa' (C + D ln(2/epsilon) + o(kappa')) equal to O(kappa' log(1/epsilon)).
quotes: the adiabatic portion prepares an “ansatz” state |xans⟩ for which |⟨xans|x⟩|2 ≥ 1/2, using at most O(κ′(A)) (controlled) queries to UA and Ub.
one obtains the state |x˜⟩ that is ε-far from |x⟩ at additional query cost O(κ′(A) log(1/ε)).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the first optimal method the constant C can be rigorously bounded as C at most 117,235 and D at most 2, that this large C dominates in practical scenarios, and that a later method with a norm-estimation step has an optimized version with C equal to 56 and D equal to 1.05, requiring b to be in the column space of A.
quotes: the constant C can be rigorously bounded as C ≤ 117,23558 and the constant D is at most 2.
An optimized version of this approach was reported to have complexity following Eq. (61) with C = 56 and D = 1.05.
one arrives at a constant 117,235, matching [9, Eq. (L2)].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for general dense matrices a classical data structure requires QRAM of O(N squared) qubits with depth O(n) per query, or as few as O(n) ancillas with depth O(N squared), and that initializing the QRAM takes O(N squared) time, while sparse or Pauli-basis matrices have more efficient block-encodings.
quotes: For general (dense) matrices A, the requirement is then size O(N 2) (number of qubits) with circuit depth O(n) for each query
Initializing the depth-efficient QRAM data structure will in general also take O(N 2) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the rigorous upper bound on the complexity constant C has been reduced by several orders of magnitude but remains larger than ideal, and that numerical investigations of two adiabatic methods on small random matrices gave evidence that empirical performance is significantly better than the rigorous bounds.
quotes: numerical investigations of two adiabatic methods on small random matrices gave evidence that the empirical performance of those methods is significantly better than the rigorous upper bounds [7].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that QLSSs do not produce a classical description of the solution, so obtaining a classical approximation requires pure state tomography with O(N epsilon^-2) samples, and that the overall complexities to obtain a classical solution can be compared with Gaussian elimination at O(N^omega), omega below 2.372, so a QLSS may not provide a superquadratic speedup when a full classical solution is extracted.
quotes: QLSSs do not produce a classical description of the solution vector x or an approximation thereof, but rather the pure quantum state |x˜⟩.

As such, it seems that the QLSS may not provide a superquadratic speedup when a full classical solution is to be extracted, and even subquadratic speedups seem to be limited to a narrow parameter regime.
which can be performed using O(N ε−2) samples.
O(N 3) or more precisely O(N ω) with ω ∈ [2, 2.372) denoting the matrix multiplication exponent.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states this caveat in Section 18 (p.290).

assertions.value: The authors state that the randomized Kaczmarz method returns an epsilon-approximation with a cost polynomial in the sparsity s and the Frobenius condition number times log of the inverse error for row-sparse matrices, and that conjugate gradient solves s-sparse positive semidefinite systems in time scaling with N s and the square root of kappa, with a quadratically worse condition number dependence for non-Hermitian matrices.
quotes: the randomized Kaczmarz method [27] with standard classical access to the matrix elements returns an ε-approximation of the vector x
at the cost of a quadratically worse condition number dependence O(N sκ log(κ(A)/ε))
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum-inspired methods with sampling access to a classical data structure give samples from an epsilon-approximation to the solution vector in complexity independent of N and polynomial in the Frobenius condition number, the condition number and the inverse error, though the required classical data structure may be prohibitively expensive to build for a huge matrix, and that quantum preconditioning is often only heuristic.
quotes: give samples from an ε-approximation to the solution vector in (N -independent) complexity
the performance of preconditioners in the quantum setting (see, e.g., [33, 34, 35, 36]) is often only heuristic, or applies only to restricted situations.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum gradient estimation algorithm evaluates the function a constant number of times in superposition over nearby grid points and uses interference to estimate the gradient, whereas classical estimation needs a number of evaluations scaling with the dimension, with the algorithm generalizing the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.
quotes: the quantum gradient estimation algorithm evaluates the function a constant number of times (in superposition over many nearby points) and uses interference effects to produce the estimate of the gradient.
The gradient estimation algorithm can be viewed as a generalization of the Bernstein– Vazirani algorithm [3]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the gradient estimation circuit uses O(d log N) qubits with gate depth independent of d, that with an evaluation oracle evaluated to precision O(epsilon/sqrt d) the circuit depth is polylogarithmic in d and the inverse error, a potentially exponential speedup over the Omega(d) classical queries, and that with a probability oracle a number of calls scaling as sqrt d over epsilon is needed.
quotes: The number of qubits is O(d log(N )), and the number of elementary operations for each of the d parallel QFTs is polylog(N )
a potentially exponential speedup over the at least Ω(d) classical query complexity to learn the gradie
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that Jordan's speedup requires a strong access model with function evaluation to high precision at cost polylogarithmic in d and the inverse error, that the cheap gradient principle in many practical situations limits the speedup, and that with a probability oracle compatible with variational algorithms only a quadratic speedup results.
quotes: the “cheap gradient principle” [4, 5] asserts that (in many practical situations) computing the gradient has roughly the same cost as computing the function itself. This principle limits the scope of application of the large speedup of Jordan’s algorithm.
which represents a (much less dramatic) quadratic speedup
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the NISQ regime structured quantum algorithms with prescribed circuits and provable guarantees are unknown, which motivated variational quantum algorithms, although VQAs could also run on fault-tolerant devices.
quotes: Under these constraints, structured quantum algorithms with prescribed circuits and provable guarantees are unknown. In light of this, variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) have been proposed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors define a variational quantum algorithm as minimizing a cost function C(theta) equal to f of the trace of O U(theta) rho U(theta)-dagger over circuit parameters theta by a classical optimizer, with a quantum computer evaluating the expectation values, aiming to offload complexity to the classical optimizer.
quotes: one evaluates C(θ) = f Tr OU (θ)ρU †(θ) on a quantum computer, which is known as a cost function.
A classical optimizer is then tasked to solve the problem
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey defines the VQA primitive in Section 20 (p.298).

assertions.value: The authors state that the cost function and ansatz should ideally satisfy: smaller cost corresponds to better solutions, the ansatz is expressive enough to contain an acceptable solution, the landscape is trainable, and the cost is classically hard to simulate, and that it can be hard to satisfy all of these simultaneously by theoretical guarantees or heuristically.
quotes: (iii) The ansatz should lead to a trainable cost landscape in parameter space
(iv) The cost function should be classically hard to simulate, given the choice of ansatz.
in general, it can be hard to satisfy all of the above requirements simultaneously via theoretical guarantees or even heuristically in practice.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' own statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that each cost evaluation approximates an expectation value to additive error epsilon with finite shots, and that epsilon should be at most O of the square root of the variance of the cost over uniformly distributed parameters in order to distinguish points on the landscape.
quotes: it should be expected that ε is at most O(
in order to accurately distinguish arbitrarily chosen points on the parameter landscape
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that optimization of certain parameterized circuits is subject to barren plateaus, where deviations between cost values vanish exponentially with the number of qubits, with the variance of the cost decaying exponentially in n, which mandates exponential shot complexity per evaluation and affects both gradient-based and gradient-free optimization, and that many standard techniques to avoid vanishing gradients render the VQA classically simulable.
quotes: in which deviations between different cost values with high probability (or deterministically, depending on the setting) vanish exponentially with increasing number of qubits
This mandates an exponential shot complexity for each evaluation of a cost value in order to reliably navigate the cost landscape
it has been found that many standard techniques to avoid vanishing gradients render the VQA classically simulable [16].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that if VQAs are run on noisy devices the effects of noise are known to severely restrict the scope for computation, amplified on devices with limited hardware connectivity.
quotes: If VQAs are run on noisy devices, the effects of noise are known to severely restrict the scope for computation [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in general there is a lack of end-to-end theoretical guarantees for variational quantum algorithms, that the classical parameter optimization is generally left as a heuristic subroutine which is in general NP-hard and can be burdened by many poor local minima, leading to a slow optimization with many cost evaluations.
quotes: Finally, in general, there is a lack of end-to-end theoretical guarantees for variational quantum algorithms.
This optimization task is in general NP-hard, and can be burdened by many local minima of poor quality [22, 23].
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states this caveat in Section 20 (p.299).

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAOA ansatz is computationally universal as p goes to infinity for certain Hamiltonian classes, that sampling from the p equal to 1 QAOA output is classically hard under reasonable complexity assumptions, that there is evidence shallow QAOA does not perform well, and that an exponential number of samples from shallow QAOA may give polynomial speedups for exactly optimal solutions.
quotes: Moreover, under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, it is known that sampling from the output of the QAOA at p = 1 is classically hard [40].
there is evidence that shallow (small p) QAOA does not perform well [41, 42, 43, 44]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational linear system solvers minimize a cost bounding the approximation error, require the matrix to decompose into a small number of efficiently implementable unitaries, and that a numerical study up to 30 qubits showed favorable scaling in time to solution with matrix size, condition number and precision.
quotes: A numerical study up to 30 qubits showed favorable scaling in the time to solution with respect to the matrix size, condition number, and precision [47].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a variational factoring method using the QAOA ansatz heuristically found that p equal to O(n) rounds can lead to a good solution overlap for small system sizes.
quotes: The authors use the QAOA ansatz and heuristically find that p = O(n) rounds of the ansatz can lead to a good solution overlap for small system sizes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational methods use a parameterized quantum circuit to construct a hypothesis family for classical or quantum data, for classification, generative models and autoencoders, with specific ansatzes sometimes called quantum neural networks, including perceptron-based QNNs, a quantum convolutional analog and tensor network approaches.
quotes: Here one employs a parameterized quantum circuit to construct a hypothesis family.
Specific ansatzes have been proposed in these contexts, sometimes referred to as quantum neural networks, in analogy with their classical counterparts.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum state tomography as obtaining a classical description of an unknown quantum state of known dimension d from repeated copies, up to an approximation error epsilon and failure probability delta, with the sample complexity in terms of the number of copies as the typical figure of merit.
quotes: In quantum tomography, often also termed quantum state estimation, we are given repeated copies of an unknown quantum state (or quantum channel)
We are then typically interested in the optimal sample complexity in terms of the number of copies n, the quantum state dimension d, the approximation error ε, and the overall failure probability δ.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey defines tomography in Section 21 (p.306).

assertions.value: The authors state that pure state tomography in l2-norm up to global phase has sample complexity Theta(d epsilon^-2), and with access to the controlled state preparation unitary and its inverse has query complexity Theta(d epsilon^-1), a quadratic speedup in 1/epsilon reminiscent of amplitude estimation.
quotes: sample complexity for pure state tomography in ℓ2-norm up to global phase [3]

query complexity for pure state tomography in ℓ2-norm with access to controlled state preparation unitary and its inverse [3], featuring a quadratic speedup in 1/ε reminiscent of amplitude estimation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that rank-k state tomography in trace distance has sample complexity of order d times k squared over epsilon squared with IID measurements and d times k over epsilon squared with entangled measurements, and query complexity of order d times k over epsilon with access to a controlled purification unitary and its inverse.
quotes: sample complexity for rank-k state tomography in trace distance with IID measurements [6, 7, 8].
sample complexity for rank-k state tomography in trace distance with entangled measurements [9, 7, 10].
query complexity for rank-k state tomography in trace distance with access to controlled state preparation unitary of a purification and its inverse [3]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sample complexity of general quantum state tomography grows exponentially in the number of qubits, so whenever tomography is a subroutine one must analyze whether it eliminates claimed speedups, and that the inverse polynomial dependence on the approximation parameter is often prohibitively expensive.
quotes: the sample complexity for general quantum state tomography grows exponentially in the number of qubits.

whenever quantum tomography is invoked as a subroutine in quantum algorithms, one has to carefully analyze if this step does not eliminate any claimed speedups of the quantum algorithm compared to state-of-the-art classical methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states the information-theoretic lower bound consequence in Section 21 (p.308).

assertions.value: The authors state that classical shadow tomography can simultaneously epsilon-approximate M linear functions of an unknown state using O(log(M) max shadow norm squared epsilon^-2) IID measurements, with the shadow norm scaling in general as d, giving worst-case O(d log(M) epsilon^-2), while for observables with bounded Hilbert-Schmidt norm or local observables a dimension-free O(log(M) epsilon^-2) is achievable.
quotes: there exist algorithmically efficient and universal schemes that can simultaneously ε-approximate M linear functions tr[Oiρ] of an unknown quantum state ρ by only using O(log(M ) · maxi ∥Oi∥s2ε−2) IID measurements.
the overall dimension-free query complexity O(log(M )ε−2) is achievable.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that since QIPMs often rely on state tomography they are generally expected to require time scaling at least linearly in the number of variables, with lower bounds known, so the best one can hope for is a polynomial speedup over classical IPMs, and that instance-specific parameters make it difficult to determine whether a speedup exists in practice.
quotes: Since QIPMs often rely on state tomography, they are generally expected to require time that scales at least linearly in the number of variables, and lower bounds along these lines are known [10]; thus, the best one can hope for is a polynomial speedup over classical IPMs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that tomography makes QIPM solutions to the Newton system inexact, that it is questioned whether the fastest-converging IPMs apply with inexact solutions, that the method appears to work empirically if the tomography precision xi is small enough, and that workarounds exist that maintain feasibility at some additional classical cost.
quotes: if ξ is sufficiently small, the method appears to work empirically even using the inexact solutions that would be output by a quantum solver [14].
there exist workarounds [12] that ensure feasibility is maintained even when linear systems are solved inexactly, at the expense of some additional classical cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of iterations T of QLSS-based QIPMs to reach an objective within epsilon of optimal is O(sqrt n) times a logarithm of the inverse precision, that each solution state is prepared in time polylog(n) times zeta kappa, and that basic tomography needs O(n/xi squared) copies for LPs and SOCPs, improvable to O(n/xi) by more complex tomography.
quotes: the number of copies that must be prepared scales as O(n/ξ2) when using the basic version
A more recent and complex version of tomography [20] can achieve this task using O(n/ξ) copies along with additional gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QIPM runtime is expected to scale as a power of n times zeta kappa over xi times a logarithm of the inverse precision, with a higher power of n for SDP than for LP and SOCP, plus an additional purely classical cost of O(n^2.5) for LPs and SOCPs and O(n^4.5) for SDPs, and that in the worst case xi might need to be as small as O(1/kappa).
quotes: There may be an additional purely classical cost of O(n2.5) for LPs/SOCPs and O(n4.5) for SDPs
it may be necessary to take ξ as small as O(1/κ)
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is believed that for some LP, SOCP and SDP instances the condition number kappa diverges as the target precision epsilon decreases, perhaps as O(1/epsilon), although not in every instance, and that the viability of the QIPM depends strongly on the value and scaling of kappa and xi.
quotes: it is believed that for some LP/SOCP/SDP instances, the value of κ will diverge as the target precision ϵ is made smaller, perhaps as O(1/ϵ) [15, 12]
It is clear that the viability of the QIPM is highly dependent on the value and scaling of the parameters κ and ξ.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QIPM needs only O(log n) qubits to hold the solution but the quoted runtimes require QRAM queries, whose explicit shallow-depth circuits of depth O(log n) necessarily require O(n squared) total gates across O(n squared) total qubits.
quotes: explicit QRAM circuits that achieve shallow depths of O(log(n)) necessarily require O(n2) total gates across O(n2) total qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that even in the best case the QIPM speedup is at most polynomial and even subquadratic, that a very large QRAM of millions or billions of logical qubits would be needed, that for small condition number iterative classical methods such as randomized Kaczmarz limit the quantum speedup to a factor O(zeta kappa), and that for the quantum speedup to be maximized kappa can be neither too small nor too large.
quotes: Even in a best case scenario, the quantum speedup is at most polynomial (and even subquadratic).
a very large QRAM, corresponding to millions or billions of (logical) qubits, would be needed for any speedup to be realized.
Thus, for the quantum speedup to be maximized, κ can be neither too small nor too large.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states these caveats in Section 22 (p.315).

assertions.value: The authors state that for portfolio optimization a study of condition numbers was consistent with a small quantum speedup but a follow-up study did not replicate it and pointed to large constant-factor overheads, and that for support vector machines a study of condition numbers was consistent with a small quantum speedup.
quotes: however, a follow-up study did not replicate this finding [14] and also pointed out that in any case large constant-factor overheads would make achieving practical advantage challenging.
a study of the condition number of the matrices that appear in this application was consistent with a small quantum speedup [15].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the multiplicative weights update method solves the promise problem of finding a feasible point or certifying infeasibility after O(log(n)/epsilon squared) iterations, that a quantum Grover search for a violated constraint speeds up each iteration giving polynomial speedups for zero-sum games and LPs, and that in typical applications the iteration count is polynomial in log n and 1/epsilon, in contrast to interior point methods.
quotes: the promise problem described above can be solved after only O(log(n)/ϵ2) iterations [1].

By searching for a violated constraint using a Grover search, the runtime of each iteration can be sped up quantumly, giving rise to polynomial speedups for solving zero-sum games and LPs more generally [3].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the matrix MWU method for SDPs maintains a density matrix that is a Gibbs state of a weighted sum of constraint matrices, so quantum algorithms can guarantee polynomial speedups per iteration with Gibbs sampling using O(s sqrt n) queries for sparsity s, and that faster-than-worst-case Gibbs sampling could conceivably give larger speedups, possibly exponential if the system thermalizes rapidly.
quotes: Thus, the quantum state X can be prepared on a quantum computer using algorithms for Gibbs sampling.
the Gibbs state ρ can typically be prepared using only O(s n) queries to the input data
representing an exponential speedup over their poly(n, 1/ϵ)-time classical counterparts.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the original quantum SDP solver based on MWU had O(epsilon^-18) dependence, later improved to O(epsilon^-5), and that this large power would likely make the algorithm worse than interior point methods with polylogarithmic scaling unless epsilon can be essentially constant, while for zero-sum games the quantum MWU algorithm has O(epsilon^-3) dependence.
quotes: The original quantum SDP solver based on MWU had O(ϵ−18) dependence [6], and this was later improved to O(ϵ−5) [4].
In the case of zero-sum games, the quantum algorithm based on the MWU method has a slightly more tolerable O(ϵ−3) dependence.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the best outlook for quantum advantage with MWU occurs when constraint matrices are sparse, ideally physical local Hamiltonians, which may not be satisfied often in practice, and that dense matrices would require large QRAM.
quotes: One caveat is that the best outlook for quantum advantage occurs when the constraint matrices A(j) that appear in applications are sparse matrices (and especially if they correspond to physical local Hamiltonians).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for any epsilon above zero a quantum algorithm for approximate tensor network contraction along a bubbling path runs in time linear in |V| and polynomial in the bond dimension and degree, with a dependence on epsilon that can be improved by amplitude estimation, and outputs a complex number within epsilon times the sequential norm Delta of the exact contraction with high probability.
quotes: there exists a quantum algorithm that runs in O(|V |ϵ−2poly(qd)) quantum time and outputs a complex number r such that [2]
Alternatively, using the amplitude estimation subroutine, the ϵ-dependence could be reduced to O(ϵ−1).
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the parameter Delta can grow exponentially with |V| and require extremely high precision to give a meaningful answer, that some tensor networks make classical additive approximation NP-hard, that families exist for which the additive approximation is BQP-hard, and that for specific partition functions the quantum scale Delta is exponential with a smaller exponent than the best known classical scheme, while the converse also occurs.
quotes: importantly though, for problems of interest is the value of ∆, which can grow exponentially with |V | and require extremely high precision
There exist families of tensor networks for which the additive approximation in Eq. (67) is BQP-hard
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, at this time, the only known problems where the quantum backend provides substantial speedup are those originating from quantum computing itself, such as random circuit sampling supremacy experiments, and that the main caveat is that the network structure allowing a significant speedup is not well understood.
quotes: At this time, however, the only known problems where the quantum backend provides substantial speedup is for problems originating from quantum computing itself
The main caveat at present is that we do not have a good understanding of the structure of the network that allows for significant speedup on a quantum computer
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' own statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the error rates of all known physical qubits and operations are too high for most of the algorithms in the survey, and that even with a minute error probability p an error is expected in any circuit with more than O(1/p) operations, so that if p = 10−6 (printed flat) were achieved, a circuit could reliably have roughly one million operations, orders of magnitude fewer than the algorithms need.
quotes: The error rates of all known realizations of physical qubits and basic operations are too high to enable implementation of the majority of quantum algorithms considered in this survey.
we would nevertheless expect an error to occur in any quantum circuit comprising more than O(1/p) operations.
One may optimistically assume that in the foreseeable future p = 10−6 might be achieved by certain quantum architectures
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the asymptotic scaling of fault tolerance overheads is manageable, polylogarithmic in the inverse target logical error rate, but the constant prefactors tend to be large, making qubit and time overheads one of the main bottlenecks to practical fault-tolerant quantum computation.
quotes: the constant prefactors tend to be large, resulting in the qubit and time overheads that currently constitute one of the main bottlenecks to practical FT quantum computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the threshold theorem asserts that there is a constant p_FT above zero such that for any epsilon and any circuit C there is a fault-tolerant circuit whose output is within statistical distance epsilon of C provided the physical error rate is below p_FT, using at most polylog(|C|/epsilon) times more qubits and time steps.
quotes: The threshold theorem asserts that there exists a constant pFT > 0, such that for any ϵ > 0 and any quantum circuit C there exists a quantum circuit C that produces an output with statistical distance at most ϵ from the output of C, provided the physical error rate p is below pFT.
uses a number of qubits and time steps that are at most polylog(|C|/ϵ) times bigger
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states the threshold theorem with its conditions in Section 25 (p.330).

assertions.value: The authors state that in the asymptotic limit of large circuits the ratio of physical to logical qubits can be a constant, using quantum low-density parity check codes with good parameters and constant-weight parity checks, but that experimental realization of such constructions seems extremely challenging for solid-state qubits with geometrically local gates.
quotes: in the asymptotic limit of large quantum circuits, the ratio of qubits in C and C can be a constant [14].
experimental realization of these constructions (in contrast to the surface code) seems to become extremely challenging as the number of physical qubits increases
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that transversal gates do not spread errors uncontrollably, but the Eastin-Knill theorem rules out a finite-dimensional QEC code with a universal set of transversal logical gates, a limitation circumvented by magic states.
quotes: Unfortunately, transversal gates are limited by the Eastin–Knill theorem [22, 23, 24, 25], which rules out the existence of a (finite-dimensional) QEC code with a universal set of transversal logical gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states the Eastin-Knill theorem in Section 25 (p.331).

assertions.value: The authors state that rigorous proofs give FT threshold lower bounds such as above 2.73 times 10^-5 for a scheme based on the 7-qubit code and above 1.04 times 10^-3 for Knill's scheme, while numerical simulations estimate a threshold as high as 5 times 10^-2 for Knill's scheme, with values depending on the noise assumptions and reduced significantly when gates are restricted to be local.

the FT scheme by Knill is estimated to have an FT threshold pFT as high as 5 × 10−2

assertions.value: The authors state that if the classical unit processing the error syndrome cannot keep pace with the rate at which it is produced, the syndrome accumulates in the so-called backlog problem, which exponentially reduces the speed of quantum computing and annuls the computational advantage, especially for algorithms with only polynomial speedups.
quotes: If the classical unit that processes the error syndrome is unable to keep pace with the rate at which this syndrome is being produced, then the error syndrome will start to accumulate and one will suffer from the so-called backlog problem [34].
This issue will be especially prominent for quantum algorithms with only polynomial speedups.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states this caveat in Section 25 (p.332).

assertions.value: The authors state that the most common surface code realization uses n equal to L squared data qubits to encode one logical qubit with code distance d equal to L on an L by L square lattice, plus L squared minus one ancilla qubits for parity check measurements, using only nearest-neighbor entangling gates.
quotes: The most common realization of the surface code uses n = L2 data qubits to encode k = 1 logical qubit and has code distance d = L
nA = L2 − 1 ancilla qubits are typically used to measure parity checks
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey defines the surface code layout in Section 26 (p.335).

assertions.value: The authors state that the surface code with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding and a depolarizing circuit noise model has a QEC threshold of around 1%, that below threshold the logical error rate scales as a power of p over p_th set by half the code distance, and that the distance needed for a target error epsilon grows logarithmically in 1/epsilon, so the qubit overhead is polylogarithmic in the inverse target error.
quotes: the QEC threshold for the surface code, using the minimum-weight perfect matching algorithm for decoding, with a circuit noise model based on depolarizing noise, is around 1% [23, 11].
it suffices to implement the surface code with code distance d = O(log(1/ϵ)/ log(pth/p))
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the three most popular surface code decoder classes are matching, clustering and tensor network decoders, that matching and clustering decoders achieve almost-linear runtime and good accuracy, and that tensor network decoders can achieve optimal accuracy but are often not computationally efficient.

matching and clustering decoders stand out. Namely, they can achieve almost-linear runtime [20, 15] and good accuracy.
To achieve optimal accuracy, one can use tensor network decoders, however, they are often not computationally efficient
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that repeated parity check measurements to handle measurement errors need O(d) rounds for the surface code of distance d, a relatively large time overhead, and that single-shot error correction with the 3D subsystem toric code trades time overhead for a qubit overhead of O(d cubed) against O(d squared).
quotes: then one needs to perform O(d) rounds of parity check measurements, incurring relatively large time overhead.
In order to realize code distance d, one incurs qubit overhead of O(d3) (compared to qubit overhead of O(d2) for the surface code).

assertions.value: The authors state that biased and erasure noise can raise QEC thresholds, while realistic coherent or correlated noise may be hard to correct and simulate, with logical error rates for coherent noise potentially orders of magnitude higher than estimates for simple Pauli noise with the same error rate, and that decoders based solely on machine learning appear of limited applicability.
quotes: the logical error rates for coherent noise may be orders of magnitude higher than the estimates of the logical error rates for simple Pauli noise (assuming both types of noise have the same error rate) [46].
decoders solely based on machine learning methods seem to be of limited applicability, mostly due to high training costs and scalability issues.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that non-Clifford gates are essential for quantum computation, since any circuit comprising only Clifford gates, state preparation and computational basis measurement can be simulated in polynomial time on a probabilistic classical computer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the logical T resource state is prepared by state distillation, converting noisy resource states into fewer, less noisy ones using Clifford circuits and postselection, often described as the main resource overhead of surface code computation, but that recent results indicate it may not be as costly, and that for estimating the Fermi-Hubbard ground state energy density distillation of Toffoli states used less than 10% of total resources.

state distillation of logical Toffoli resource states injected one at a time uses less than 10% of the total resources and is never a bottleneck on runtime of the quantum algorithm [23].

assertions.value: The authors state that the gate set of single-qubit X, Y, Z, H and S gates with CNOT generates the Clifford group, which is not universal and whose computations can be efficiently simulated classically, so significant quantum speedups cannot come from Clifford gates alone, while adding the T gate or the Toffoli gate makes the set universal.
quotes: Importantly, quantum computations on n qubits involving only Clifford gates can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer; thus, significant quantum computational speedups cannot be achieved using only Clifford gates.
By adding either the T gate or the Toffoli gate to the generating set, the gate set becomes universal.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the Clifford plus T gate set it is common to ignore Clifford gates and count only T or Toffoli gates, because non-Clifford gates are more difficult to implement than Clifford gates in many schemes for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
quotes: it is common to ignore the Clifford gates and only count the non-Clifford gates, that is, the T gates (or the Toffoli gates). The main reason for this is that non-Clifford gates are more difficult to implement than Clifford gates in many (but not all) schemes for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey states its counting convention in Appendix B (p.354).

assertions.value: The authors state that a resource estimate for the ideal logical circuit can be converted into a resource estimate for the actual physical quantum computer by a calculation that depends on the hardware and the fault-tolerance scheme, and that the survey focuses on fault-tolerant algorithms and logical resource estimates, commenting on NISQ algorithms in passing.

While the focus of this survey is on quantum algorithms for fault-tolerant quantum computers and logical resource estimates, we comment in passing on NISQ algorithms for many of the tasks.

assertions.value: The authors define an exponential speedup as Q(n) equal to O(log C(n)), a polynomial speedup of degree d as Q(n) equal to O(C(n)^(1/d)), and a superpolynomial speedup as meeting the polynomial criterion for all d at least 1 but not the exponential one, and state that end-to-end analyses should also assess omitted constant prefactors.

If Q(n) and C(n) meet the criterion for a polynomial speedup for all d ≥ 1 but not the criterion for an exponential speedup, then we say the speedup is superpolynomial.

assertions.value: The authors define P, BPP, BQP, NP and QMA as classes of decision problems solvable or verifiable in polynomial time by deterministic, randomized, quantum, classical verification and quantum verification algorithms, and state that showing a problem NP-hard or QMA-hard is strong evidence it does not admit an efficient quantum algorithm, while BQP-completeness is evidence of a superpolynomial quantum speedup.

showing that a problem is NP-hard or QMA-hard is strong evidence that it does not admit an efficient quantum algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that complexity-theoretic results typically concern worst-case hardness and may not be relevant for real-world instances, giving the example that local-Hamiltonian ground state preparation is QMA-complete although efficient preparation is expected for many Hamiltonians arising in nature, which forms the basis for many proposed applications.

assertions.value: The authors state that oracles enable modular accounting of algorithm costs by multiplying the number of queries by the cost of one query, that in end-to-end analyses all oracles must be instantiated with elementary operations, and that oracle separations such as Simon's problem give unconditional exponential separations in query complexity but do not alone constitute a definitive quantum advantage in end-to-end complexity.
